title: 堆叠能胜过你的最佳模型吗？
author: Himanshu Sharma
content:
Machine Learning

It only helps when your models make different mistakes.

Himanshu Sharma
October 14, 20266 min read

The theoretical case for stacking

Ensembling is close to gospel in competitive ML: stack a handful of models, feed their predictions into a meta-model that learns how to combine them, and you generally beat any single model in the stack. The theoretical mechanism is specific, not vague: it works when the base models make different kinds of errors. If model A gets right what model B gets wrong, a meta-model can learn to trust each one where it's reliable. If all the base models make the same errors, there's nothing complementary to combine, and stacking should buy you little to nothing.

That's a testable, falsifiable claim, not just "stacking is good," but specifically "stacking's benefit scales with how differently your base models err." So I built two conditions on the same dataset, one designed to give stacking real room to help and one designed to take that room away, and measured what actually happened. Every result below comes from repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation (3 repeats, 15 total folds) rather than a single train/test split — a robustness fix for a limitation flagged in an earlier benchmark of mine, where single-split numbers can move around more than they should.

Dataset: a synthetic binary classification problem (sklearn.datasets.make_classification, 2,000 samples, 20 features, realistic noise and class overlap) — clearly synthetic, chosen so the base-model diversity could be controlled directly rather than being an accident of whatever real dataset happened to be lying around.

Condition 1 — diverse base models, the setup stacking's theory is built on: logistic regression (linear), a decision tree (axis-aligned splits), an SVM (kernel-based, a fundamentally different decision boundary), and k-nearest-neighbors (instance-based, no explicit boundary at all). Four genuinely different ways of drawing a decision boundary.

Condition 2 — correlated base models, deliberately working against stacking's theory: random forest, gradient boosting, and extra-trees — three variants of the same underlying idea (tree ensembles), likely to agree with each other far more than the diverse group does.

The results

In the diverse condition, stacking earned its keep. 0.830 versus the best single model's 0.820 — a real, meaningful gap given the error bars (±0.015 for stacking, ±0.012 for the single model) barely overlap. This is stacking behaving exactly the way its theoretical case predicts: four models making genuinely different kinds of mistakes gave the meta-model real complementary signal to combine.

In the correlated condition, stacking's edge nearly vanished. 0.835 versus 0.834 — a 0.1-point difference that's completely swallowed by the standard deviation on either number (±0.014 and ±0.019 respectively). Three tree-ensemble variants agree with each other closely enough that there was almost nothing left for a meta-model to exploit. This is the theory's own prediction, confirmed directly: no error diversity, no stacking benefit.

The surprise: voting underperformed the best single model in both conditions. Not stacking — plain averaging. 0.809 versus 0.820 in the diverse condition, 0.829 versus 0.834 in the correlated one. Simple voting has no way to down-weight a genuinely weaker model in the mix; it just averages everyone in, including whichever base model is dragging the group down. Stacking's meta-model, by contrast, learns how much to trust each base model — which is exactly why it didn't suffer the same fate.

The cost side of the ledger

In the diverse condition, stacking's 23.7 seconds for a genuine 1-point accuracy gain is a reasonable trade in most real settings. In the correlated condition, it's a much harder sell: 125.9 seconds — roughly 35x the single model's training time — for a 0.1-point difference that isn't statistically distinguishable from zero. That's not a rounding error in a research paper; in a pipeline that retrains regularly, it's a real, recurring cost paid for nothing.

Why voting lost even when stacking won

This deserves its own explanation, because it's the least intuitive result here. Voting and stacking use the same base models — the only difference is how they're combined. Voting takes a fixed, equal-weighted average of every base model's prediction. Stacking trains a second model whose entire job is to learn the right weighting, informed by which base models are actually reliable on which kinds of examples.

In the diverse condition, KNN and the plain decision tree were the weakest of the four base models — solid but clearly behind the SVM. Voting has no mechanism to notice that and downweight them; it just averages all four in in equal proportion, and the weaker two drag the ensemble below what the strongest single model achieved on its own. Stacking's meta-model, trained on out-of-fold predictions from all four, learns something closer to "trust the SVM more, the tree less" — which is precisely the mechanism that let it beat the best single model instead of getting dragged down by the weakest one.

Where this comparison falls short

  • One synthetic dataset. The diversity-versus-correlation pattern is a property of ensemble theory in general, not this dataset specifically, but the exact numbers (the size of stacking's edge, the size of voting's shortfall) would shift on real, messier data with a different noise profile.

  • Base model choices, not an exhaustive search. A different choice of four "diverse" models, or three "correlated" ones, could shift these specific numbers — though the underlying mechanism (diversity creates room for a meta-model to add value) should hold regardless of which specific models embody "diverse" versus "correlated."

  • Binary classification only. Multi-class or regression stacking can behave differently, particularly around how the meta-model's cross-validation is structured.

The actual decision framework

Before reaching for a stacking ensemble over your single best model, three questions:

  1. Do your candidate base models actually make different kinds of errors, or do they just have different names? Three tree-ensemble variants sound diverse but often aren't, in the way that actually matters for stacking. Check correlation between base models' predictions (or errors) before assuming diversity — it's one line of code and it directly predicts how much stacking will help.

  2. Is the accuracy gain, if any, larger than your fold-to-fold noise? A single train/test split will happily report a stacking "win" that's actually just noise — cross-validate and look at the spread, not just the mean, before trusting a comparison like this one.

  3. What's the actual cost of retraining a stack versus a single model, at your real retraining frequency? 126 seconds once is nothing. 126 seconds every night for a year, for a gain within the noise floor, is a cost worth naming explicitly rather than paying by default.

The takeaway

"Stacking beats your best single model" is true under a specific, checkable condition — genuine diversity in how the base models err — and considerably less true outside it. The more interesting and more actionable finding here isn't stacking versus single models in the abstract; it's that naive voting can actually underperform your best individual model even when stacking, using the exact same base models, doesn't. Combining models isn't free, and averaging isn't the same as combining well — the meta-model's ability to learn who to trust and when is doing real work that a simple average can't replicate.

summary: 本文通过将模型堆叠与单一最佳模型和投票集成进行比较，来研究模型堆叠的有效性。它表明，当基础模型本质上不同时（例如，线性、树、SVM、KNN），堆叠会大幅提高准确率（0.830 vs 0.820）；但当模型过于相似时（例如，三个基于树的变体），堆叠则无法改善性能（0.835 vs 0.834）。此外，投票集成始终表现不佳于单一最佳模型，这突出了元模型在学习组合权重时的重要性。

mainPoints.point: 堆叠需要错误多样性才能有效。
mainPoints.explanation: 在'多样化基础模型'条件下观察到的显著性能提升（0.830 vs 0.820）表明，当基础模型犯下不同类型的错误时，堆叠最有效，因为元模型可以利用它们互补的优势。在'相关基础模型'条件下，由于模型过于相似，堆叠的增益是统计学上不显著的（0.835 vs 0.834），这说明集成无法在错误模式没有足够差异的情况下超越单个最佳模型。
在两种实验条件下，投票集成（0.809 和 0.829）都一致地表现不佳于单个最佳模型（0.820 和 0.834）。这是因为投票将所有模型视为同等重要，没有考虑到单个分类器的相对质量或错误特点，而堆叠则会根据每个模型的性能学习最优权重。

mainPoints.point: 堆叠的计算成本必须由其增益来平衡。
mainPoints.explanation: 虽然堆叠可以提高准确率，但它也会带来显著的计算惩罚。在相关模型条件下，堆叠训练时间为 125.9 秒，而单个最佳模型仅需 3.6 秒。考虑到这种情况下的准确率提升可以忽略不计（仅 0.1 分），额外的计算成本是不划算的，因此，单一模型是更有效率的选择。

keyQuotes: 理论机制很具体，而不是模糊的：当基础模型犯下*不同*类型的错误时，它才会起作用。
在多样化的条件下，堆叠证明了自己的价值。0.830 相比单个最佳模型的 0.820——这是一个真实且有意义的差距。
在相关的条件下，堆叠的优势几乎消失了。0.835 相比 0.834——0.1 分的差异完全被任何一个数的标准差所吞没。
令人惊讶的是：在两种条件下，投票集成都表现出了低于单个最佳模型的水平。
